content: Amebiasis is an infectious disease caused by the parasite Entamoeba histolytica. This condition is more prevalent in individuals residing in tropical regions with inadequate sanitation or those traveling to such areas. Antibiotic therapy is effective in treating amebiasis. The parasite Entamoeba histolytica primarily infects the small intestine of humans. While anyone can contract amebiasis, the risk is significantly higher for individuals living in or traveling to tropical areas with poor hygiene and sanitation. If you suspect you have amebiasis, it is essential to consult a healthcare provider, as the disease can be challenging to diagnose. Although most individuals with amebiasis do not experience severe symptoms, all infected individuals should receive appropriate medical treatment to eliminate the infection. Approximately 10% to 20% of individuals infected with E. histolytica develop symptoms, which are often mild. These symptoms may include diarrhea, abdominal pain, and cramping. Symptoms typically appear within 2 to 4 weeks of infection but can sometimes manifest later. In severe cases, a condition known as amebic dysentery may occur, characterized by abdominal pain, bloody stools, and fever. Rarely, the parasite can spread through the bloodstream to the liver, leading to the formation of an abscess (a collection of pus). In very rare cases, the infection may disseminate to other organs, such as the lungs or brain. In the United States, individuals at higher risk for amebiasis include those who have traveled to tropical regions with poor sanitation, immigrants from such areas, residents of facilities with inadequate hygiene, and individuals who engage in anal sexual activity. Amebiasis is transmitted through the ingestion of E. histolytica cysts. This can occur by consuming contaminated food or water, placing objects in the mouth that have been in contact with feces from an infected person, or ingesting the parasite from contaminated surfaces or hands. Preventing amebiasis involves practicing good hygiene, particularly thorough handwashing with soap and water after using the restroom, changing diapers, or before handling food or drinks. If you are in an area with poor sanitation, avoid consuming fountain drinks, ice cubes, unpeeled fresh fruits or vegetables, unpasteurized dairy products, and food or beverages sold by street vendors. Safe drinking options include bottled water with intact seals, carbonated beverages from sealed containers, or tap water that has been boiled for at least one minute. Alternatively, tap water can be made safe by filtering it through an absolute 1 micron or less filter and then treating it with chlorine, chlorine dioxide, or iodine tablets. To diagnose amebiasis, a healthcare provider will request stool samples, often collected over several days, as the parasite may not be present in every sample. Diagnosing E. histolytica can be challenging because other parasites and cells may appear similar under a microscope. If you are asymptomatic but have been diagnosed with E. histolytica, it is possible that you are infected with Entamoeba dispar, a related but non-pathogenic parasite that does not require treatment. Advanced diagnostic tests, available in some laboratories including the CDC, can differentiate between E. histolytica and E. dispar. In cases of liver abscesses, fluid from the abscess can also be tested for E. histolytica. Treatment for amebiasis involves the use of antibiotics prescribed by a healthcare provider. If you are asymptomatic, a single antibiotic may be sufficient. However, if you are symptomatic, you will likely need to take a second antibiotic after completing the first course to ensure complete eradication of the infection.
